header: For Appellant Mr. Amir Javed, Advocate
For Federation Mr. Fasih Ullah, Asst; Attorney
For Respondents Mr. Farman Ullah Khattak,
J U D G M E N T
body: ****** BABAR SATTAR, J. This is an appeal under Section 39 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 (“Arbitration Act”), against the judgment dated 04.06.2026, whereby the application filed by the appellant under Sections 20 and 46 of the Arbitration Act, read with Rule 49 of the Public Procurement Rules, 2004 (“PPRA Rules”), was dismissed.

2. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the appellant had participated in a tender process undertaken pursuant to the PPRA Rules. The appellant was declared a successful bidder and was issued a work order by respondent No. 2 pursuant to a contract agreement dated 28.11.2025 between the appellant and respondent No. 1 (“Agreement”). He submitted that, while the appellant had discharged his obligations under the Agreement, the same was unilaterally terminated on 05.05.2026. As the procurement process was regulated by the PPRA framework, any dispute between the parties arising out of the Agreement was required to be settled through mandatory arbitration in terms of Rule 49(1) of the PPRA Rules. The appellant served a notice for arbitration upon the respondents on 07.05.2026. But when they failed to refer the matter to arbitration, the appellant filed an application under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, seeking reference of the dispute to arbitration. He further submitted that the respondents filed an application for dismissal of the appellant’s application, which was allowed by the learned Additional District Judge, and the appellant’s application was dismissed on the ground that there was no arbitration clause in the Agreement. While an arbitration clause ought to have been included in the Agreement in terms of Rule 49(2) of the PPRA Rules by respondent No.2, the same had not been incorporated. He submitted that Section 46 of the Arbitration Act provided that the provisions of the Arbitration Act would apply to any arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force. The Public Procurement Regulatory Authority Ordinance, 2002 (“PPRA Ordinance”), under which the PPRA Rules were framed, constituted such an enactment as contemplated by Section 46 of the Arbitration Act. As Rule 49 was mandatory in nature and required disputes arising under procurement contracts to be settled through arbitration, the appellant had no remedy but to seek adjudication of his dispute through arbitration. He further submitted that the learned Additional District Judge had failed to distinguish between voluntary arbitration arising out of an arbitration agreement between the parties, and statutory arbitration mandated by a statutory provision even in the absence of an arbitration agreement between the parties. Learned counsel for the appellant relied upon the following judgments in support of the proposition that statutory arbitration is binding even in the absence of an arbitration clause in the contract between the parties: Bihar Industrial Area Development Authority & Ors. v. Rama Kant Singh (2022 INSC 308), Brooke Bond (Pakistan) Ltd. v. Conciliator appointed by the Government of Sindh (PLD 1977 SC 237), and M/s. Gayatri Project Limited v. Madhya Pradesh (2025 INSC 698).

3. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that the appellant had failed to discharge his obligations to provide goods in terms of the provisions of the Agreement, which was consequently rescinded on 05.05.2026. The Agreement did not contain an arbitration clause. In the absence of an arbitration agreement between the parties, the dispute could not be referred to arbitration under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act, as rightly held by the learned Additional District Judge. He submitted that Rule 49 was not mandatory, as it did not provide any penalty for non-compliance. At best, it was a directory provision requiring a procuring agency to include an arbitration clause in the procurement contract. However, where no such clause had been incorporated into the Agreement, there was no meeting of minds or agreement between the parties to refer their disputes arising out of the Agreement to arbitration, as correctly held by the learned Additional District Judge.

4. The appellant, as a private party, entered into a supply agreement with respondent No. 2, which is a state-owned entity, through a bidding process undertaken in accordance with the PPRA Ordinance and the PPRA Rules. The appellant filed an application under Section 20 of the Arbitration Act for appointment of an arbitrator on the basis that, while the Agreement did not contain an arbitration clause, arbitration was mandatory due to the incorporation by statute of such a requirement under Rule 49(1) of the PPRA Rules, even where the respondent, as a procuring agency, had failed to comply with the requirement of Rule 49(2) of the PPRA Rules to incorporate an arbitration clause in the Agreement. The appellant accordingly argues that, by virtue of Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules, read with Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, an arbitration agreement stands incorporated by statutory diktat. The respondent argues that there is no arbitration clause in the Agreement between the parties. Even if the respondent, as a procuring agency, has not complied with Rule 49(2) of the PPRA Rules, there is no mandatory arbitration agreement in place, as no such contractual arrangement was agreed upon by the parties. It is further argued that the PPRA Rules cannot be treated as an enactment in terms of Section 3(17) of the General Clauses Act, 1897, as, in jurisdictions where statutory arbitration is given effect, it is the statute itself that requires and mandates arbitration between the parties, which is something that neither the Arbitration Act nor the PPRA Ordinance, read with the PPRA Rules, does. The contesting argument to the appellant’s assertion, therefore, is that arbitration as a mandatory disputeresolution mechanism requires the consent of the parties, which is absent here, and that, by virtue of Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules, mandatory arbitration ousting the jurisdiction of civil courts in terms of Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”), cannot be implied.

5. The question before this Court is purely a question of law, as the facts are not disputed. The appellant participated in a tender process initiated by respondent No.1, and was issued a work order as the successful bidder, whereafter the parties entered into the Agreement. Admittedly, the Agreement does not contain an arbitration clause, nor does it incorporate any other bidding documents containing such a clause. The sole basis of the appellant’s claim is that Rule 49 provides for mandatory arbitration in the event of a dispute arising between a successful bidder and a procuring agency under a contract awarded through the procurement process. The appellant’s case is that Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules is to be construed as providing for mandatory statutory arbitration contemplated by Section 46 of the Arbitration Act. In this regard, Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules provides as follows:
49. Arbitration- (1) After coming into force of the procurement contracts, disputes between the parties to the contract shall be settled by arbitration.
(2) The procuring agencies shall provide for a method of arbitration in the procurement contract, not inconsistent with the laws of Pakistan.
It will also be useful to reproduce Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, which provides as follows:

46. Application of Act to statutory arbitrations. The provisions of this Act, except sub-section (1) of section 6 and section 7, 12, 1 [,36] and 37, shall apply to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, as if the arbitration were pursuant to an arbitration agreement and as if that other enactment were an arbitration agreement, except in so far as this Act is inconsistent with that other enactment or with any rules made thereunder.

For convenience, the definitions of “enactment”, “regulation” and “rule” under the General Clauses Act, 1897, which are relevant for interpreting the term “enactment” for the purposes of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, are also reproduced below:

Section. 3(17) "Enactment" shall include a Regulation (as hereinafter defined) and any Regulation of the Bengal, 55*** or Bombay Code, and shall also include any provision contained in any Act or in any such Regulation as aforesaid.

(46) "Regulation" "Regulation" shall mean a Regulation made [by the Central Government] under the Government of India Act, 1870, [or the Government of India Act, 1915.] [or the Government of India Ac] [or under section 95 or section 96 of the Government of India Act. 1935] [or by the Governor under Article 103 or Article 104 of the Constitution of 1956, or by the President or by the Governor under Article 223 of the Constitution of 1962] [,or by the President or by the Governor under Article 247 of the Constitution of 1973] (47) "Rule" "Rule" shall mean a rule made in exercise of a power conferred by any enactment, and shall include a regulation made as a rule under any enactment.

6. Before considering the rival arguments of the parties, it is appropriate to revisit the rationale of arbitration and how private arbitration is distinguishable from statutory arbitration. Arbitration as a disputeresolution mechanism predates the formal court system. It was relied upon by traders and merchants to settle disputes long before court systems came to be established as the primary dispute-resolution mechanism. Even after the establishment of courts, arbitration has continued to gain currency as a preferred dispute-resolution mechanism because it underscores party autonomy, enables contracting parties to choose an arbitrator with relevant expertise to understand the dispute and its technicalities, and as a dispute-resolution system preserves privacy and promotes the expeditious resolution of disputes, with arbitral awards treated as decisions clothed with finality (subject of course to court intervention based on considerations that vary from one jurisdiction to another). The argument that parties could oust the jurisdiction of courts by private agreement was not readily accepted by the courts. The resistance may have been inspired by institutional interests and turfmarking. In the post-industrial revolution world, however, the benefits of private dispute resolution came to be recognized. The seminal case credited with marking the end of the courts’ hostility to arbitration was Scott Vs. Avery ((1855) 5 HL Case 811). In this case, the House of Lords recognized that parties can lawfully contract that an arbitration award shall be a condition precedent for a contracting party to assert its right to sue. Thereafter, various statutes were introduced that codified this shift in attitude, such as the English Arbitration Act, 1899, the Indian Arbitration Act, 1899, and the Arbitration Act, 1940, which is still in force in Pakistan. Within the jurisprudence that has evolved under arbitration law, it is evident that deference to arbitration is, in fact, deference to party autonomy and giving effect to the common intention of contracting parties where they agree to subject their disputes to a private adjudicatory arrangement. Arbitration rests on the private choice of parties as documented in an arbitration agreement. It is stated in Redfern and Hunter on International Arbitration (5th edition, OUP, 2009, chapter 2, pp. 84) that “the agreement to arbitrate is the foundation stone” of arbitration. (See also Gary Born’s International Commercial Arbitration (3rd edition, Kluwer) for the consensual nature of arbitration, and Russell on Arbitration (24th edition, Sweet & Maxwell, 2015) for the distinction between private and statutory arbitration, with the enactment, in the context of statutory arbitration, being regarded as the arbitration agreement).

7. The Arbitration Act does not provide a separate procedural mechanism for statutory arbitrations. Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, reproduced above, merely acknowledges that the procedural machinery established by the Arbitration Act would apply directly to every arbitration under any other enactment for the time being in force, subject to the limitations specified therein. It further provides that in the case of statutory arbitration, the enactment itself is to be treated as an arbitration agreement. Section 2(a) of the Arbitration Act defines an arbitration agreement as “a written agreement to submit present or future differences to arbitration whether an arbitrator is named therein or not.”

8. Statutory arbitration, on the other hand, is a product of public policy and overrides party autonomy. Statutory arbitration creates a jurisprudential paradox. It discards the basic premise on which arbitration is founded i.e., party autonomy and bilateral consent. This form of arbitration creates a legal fiction that the parties have agreed to arbitrate. But it is the legislature that wills, instead of the parties, that they must arbitrate. Consequently, the arbitral tribunal in the context of statutory arbitration is in the nature of a specialized statutory or administrative tribunal. It is the legislature’s directive that replaces the consent of the parties in statutory arbitration. Thus, the jurisdiction-vesting mandate must flow clearly from the words used by the legislature where statutory arbitration is intended to act as the prescribed dispute-resolution mechanism ousting the plenary jurisdiction of civil courts. Mandatory statutory arbitration seeks to borrow the procedure of private arbitration, which is credited with being devoid of delayinducing formality, to advance the policy objectives of the legislature. The focus thus shifts from the autonomy of the parties and their consent, to legislative intent as manifested by the language of the statute. Having touched upon party autonomy and consent as the raison d’être of arbitration, and legislative intent and policy as the basis for mandatory statutory arbitration, let us now consider the regime established under the PPRA Ordinance and the PPRA Rules, and whether it mandates arbitration for the resolution of post-award disputes between a procuring agency and a successful bidder.

9. The power of the Court to appoint an arbitrator in terms of Section 8 of the Arbitration Act also refers to an arbitration agreement. Section 20 of the Arbitration Act identifies an arbitration agreement as a necessary precondition for an application before the Court to have a dispute referred to arbitration. Section 21 of the Arbitration Act enables parties to a dispute to refer the subject matter of the dispute to arbitration during the pendency of a suit by mutual agreement, in which case the appointment of the arbitrator is to be made in such manner as agreed between the parties. Section 34 of the Arbitration Act similarly enables a party to an arbitration agreement to apply to the Court to stay proceedings and have the matter referred to arbitration, so long as the dispute falls within the scope of the arbitration agreement. This entire scheme reflects that the consent of the parties, as reflected in the arbitration agreement, forms the cornerstone of the framework within which arbitration takes place. Section 46 of the Arbitration Act is an exception to this rule, as, by legal fiction, it replaces an arbitration agreement with the provision of an enactment that mandates arbitration.

10. The term “enactment”, being the key word in Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, takes us to its definition. Under Section 3(17) of the General Clauses Act, the definition of “enactment”, reproduced above, while including “Regulation” (also a defined term), does not include “Rule”. This is important because “Regulation” and “Rule” are both defined terms under Sections 3(46) and 3(47) of the General Clauses Act, respectively. A combined reading of these definitions makes it evident that for the purposes of the definition of “enactment” in the General Clauses Act, a rule is not included therein. The exclusion of “rule” from the definition of “enactment” becomes even more pertinent because Section 46 of the Arbitration Act itself refers to an enactment at least twice. The first use acknowledges that, where an enactment mandates arbitration, it would be deemed that an arbitration agreement exists, as a legal fiction created by Section 46. The second use of the term “enactment” in Section 46 of the Arbitration Act emphasizes that, where there exists any inconsistency between the provisions of the Arbitration Act and the enactment providing for statutory arbitration, the provisions of the latter shall prevail. It also provides that such inconsistency may be between the Arbitration Act and the other enactment or “with any rules made thereunder”. The mention of rules along with the second use of the term “enactment” highlights that the exclusion of rules alongside the first use of the same term in Section 46 of the Arbitration Act is deliberate. Thus, the legislature specifically referred to rules in the said provision where it wished to do so, and it can, therefore, not be implied that for the purposes of Section 46, the legislature treated rules made under an enactment as part of the term “enactment” itself. While interpreting statutes, the rule against surplusage and the presumption of meaningful variation apply. If "enactment" already included rules, the words "or with any rules made thereunder" in the second part of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act would add nothing. It is a settled principle of statutory interpretation that the legislature is not presumed to use words in vain. And where a draftsman includes a term in one part of a provision and leaves it out in another, the omission is presumed to be deliberate.
11. The Supreme Court, while interpreting the definition of “enactment” under Section 3(17) of the General Clauses Act in Mst. Hamida Begum v. Mst. Murad Begum (PLD 1975 SC 624), noted that:

“the term "enactment" is defined in clause (17) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act as including "Regulation and any Regulation of the Bengal or Bombay Code, and shall also include any provision contained in any Act or in any such Regulation as aforesaid." The term "Regulation" itself is defined in clause (46) of the same section as meaning a Regulation made by the Central Government under the successive Government of India Acts of 1870, 1915 or 1935. In other words, the term "enactment" connotes something which has been formally promulgated or enacted by an authority having the power to make laws in respect of the subject-matter of the law as well as its territorial operation. To put it differently, the term "enactment" can only refer to a formal law made by the State in accordance with the relevant Constitutional procedures applicable to law-making; it cannot extend to anything in the nature of rules, whether of evidence or substantive law. not contained in any statute, Regulation or Act formally promulgated or enacted.”

In view of the interpretation of the term “enactment” under the General Clauses Act, which definition applies for the purposes of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, rules framed under an enactment are not deemed to form part of the enactment or to fall within the definition of “enactment”. This is relevant for our purposes because the appellant seeks to rely on Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules to argue that the Rules, while mandating arbitration, are to be treated as an “enactment” for the purposes of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act.

12. A plain textual reading of the definitions, together with Section 46 of the Arbitration Act, distinguishes between an enactment and rules. In view of the interpretation provided by the Supreme Court in Mst. Hamida Begum, an enactment refers to the formal law enacted by the State and does not include rules framed by the executive in exercise of authority delegated by the legislature. This distinction is relevant because, ordinarily, rules framed in exercise of delegated authority are recognized as having statutory force. This principle, however, is subject to the further principle that statutory rules cannot enlarge the scope of the section under which they are framed, as a delegatee exercising delegated power cannot go beyond the four corners of the statute. It was held by the Supreme Court in Pakistan v. Aryan Petro Chemical Industries (Pvt.) (2003 SCMR 370) that: “a statutory rule cannot enlarge the scope of the section under which it is framed and if a rule goes beyond what the section contemplates, the rule must yield to the statute. The authority of executive make rules and regulations in order to effectuate the intention and policy of the Legislature, must be exercised within the limits of mandate given to the rule making authority and the rules framed under an enactment must be consistent with the provisions of said enactment. The rules framed under a statue if are inconsistent with the provisions of the statute and defeat the intention of the Legislature expressed in the main suit, same shall be invalid. The rule making authority cannot clothe itself with power which is not given to it under the statutes and thus the rules made under a statute neither enlarge the scope of act nor can go beyond the act and must not be in conflict with the provisions of statute or repugnant to any other law in force.”

13. Let us now consider the PPRA Ordinance and its scope. The preamble of the Ordinance provides that the Public Procurement Regulatory Authority (“PPRA”) has been established “for regulating procurement of goods, services, works and disposal of public assets in the public sector and for matters connected therewith or ancillary thereto.” Section 26 of the PPRA Ordinance vests in the Federal Government the power to make rules, pursuant to which the PPRA Rules have been framed. Section 20-A of the PPRA Ordinance provides that “the procuring agency shall, by rules and regulations made under this ordinance, have a mechanism for grievance redressal of bidder during procurement.” Under the PPRA Rules, a bidder is defined as a person who submits a bid, whereas a contractor is separately defined as a bidder who has signed a contract with the procuring agency. There is no provision in the PPRA Ordinance that mandates the provision of a disputeresolution mechanism for the administration of a contract entered into between a procuring agency and a contractor. As a matter of fact, Section 20-A of the PPRA Ordinance only contemplates the provision of a mechanism for grievance redressal for bidders but not for contractors. It is against this backdrop that we need to consider whether Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules is mandatory or directory, quite apart from the question of whether rules form part of an enactment, which has already been considered above.

14. There is considerable case law on when a statutory direction is to be considered directory as opposed to mandatory. One of the initial cases in which the distinction was explained by the Supreme Court was Chief Commissioner v. Jamil Ahmed (PLD 1961 SC 145). The question before the Supreme Court concerned the scope of Section 280(1) of the City of Karachi Municipal Act, 1933, and whether the period prescribed therein relating to notification of the general elections was directory or mandatory. The Supreme Court relied on and reproduced the arguments of the Attorney General, who had relied on texts from various treatises on statutory interpretation, including Crawford’s Statutory Construction, (1940 edition, p. 529), which provides that “as a general rule statute which regulates the manner in which public officials shall exercise the power vested in them, will be construed as directory rather than mandatory.” The Supreme Court also relied on Maxwell's Interpretation of Statutes (6th edition, pp. 649–50), which provides that “where the prescriptions relate to the performance of a public duty; and to invalidate acts done in neglect of them would work serious general inconvenience or injustice to persons who have no control over those entrusted with the duty, without promoting the essential aims of the legislature, such prescriptions seem to be generally understood as mere instructions for the guidance and government of those on whom the duty is imposed, or, in other words, as directory only.”

15. The two matters for our consideration, therefore, are the overall scope of the PPRA Ordinance and whether the prescription in Rule 49, providing that any differences between a procuring agency and a contractor be referred to arbitration, is directory or mandatory. The procurement of goods and services in the public realm and the distribution of public resources by the State have long been recognized as matters falling within the public realm. The post-award relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor, however, is regulated by the contract between the parties. This relationship is ordinarily considered to fall within the domain of private law rather than public law. There are limited exceptions to this rule, including those identified in Messrs Airport Support Services v. The Airport Manager & Others (1998 SCMR 2268), highlighting that, where the State acts in breach of contract in a manner that vitiates due process or infringes other fundamental rights of a private party, such conduct may fall within the exception to the rule that the High Court does not ordinarily take cognizance of contractual disputes in its constitutional jurisdiction. In the postaward relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor, disputes that arise are determined and adjudicated pursuant to the provisions of the Contract Act, 1872, and the Specific Relief Act, 1877, read with the terms of the contract agreement. Such disputes are ordinarily agitated through a suit filed before the civil court or through contractual arbitration, if expressly agreed upon between the parties. Within this broader distinction, whereby procurement law is a subset of public law and the post-award contractual relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor falls within the domain of private law, we can return to the question of whether Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules is to be treated as mandatory or directory. (Let us clarify that the question whether Rule 49, which seeks to regulate the post-award relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor, falls beyond the four corners of the PPRA Ordinance is not before us and can be considered in an appropriate case.)

16. Learned counsel for the appellant relied on various judgments issued by Indian Courts that are of no avail to the appellant. A detailed resume of such cases need not be provided here, as that will unnecessarily burden this judgment. The question in the judgments cited related to ironing out the inconsistencies between the provisions of enactments providing for statutory arbitration and the provisions of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. It is in such context that, in view of the relevant provisions of the arbitration law in force in India, the courts held that the provisions of the enactment providing for statutory arbitration, being a special law, would override the provisions of the general arbitration law. Some of the cases also considered the question of incorporation of an arbitration agreement by reference. None of those cases, however, are relevant to the question before us. It is not in contention have that statutory arbitration can be mandated by the legislature, as has been done through Section 54 of the Cooperative Societies Act, 1925. The question before us is limited to whether Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules mandates statutory arbitration.

17. We have considered the scope of the PPRA Ordinance and the aforementioned distinction between public law and private law in relation to the pre-award and post-award relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor for the purpose of explaining the relevant legislative intent manifested by Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules. As aforementioned, PPRA Act does seek to regulate the post-award relationship between a procuring agency and a contractor. Rule 49(1) requires that disputes between the parties to a contract “shall be settled by arbitration.” Rule 49(2) then directs procuring agencies to “provide for a method of arbitration in the procurement contract, not inconsistent with the laws of Pakistan.” A combined reading of Rule 49 requires the procuring agency to include within the contract to be executed with the contractor an arbitration agreement requiring the parties to resolve any disputes arising under the contract through arbitration. Rule 49 does not, in itself, prescribe a penalty for the non-inclusion of an arbitration agreement in the contract. Within the scheme of the PPRA Rules, the only possible consequence of non-compliance with the directive would be that the award may be deemed to be a product of misprocurement. Such an outcome would, however, be absurd, as the failure of a procuring agency to comply with a direction to include an arbitration agreement in the contract would have the effect of annulling the award itself for no fault of the successful bidder. Such an illogical outcome cannot be contemplated, especially in a context where the PPRA Ordinance itself does not seek to regulate the post-award relationship between the procuring agency and the contractor. We accordingly find that Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules is directory and not mandatory.

18. The final matter that we must now consider is the effect of interpreting Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules as an “enactment” for the purposes of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act providing for mandatory arbitration, which would operate as an ouster of the plenary jurisdiction of the civil courts for the purposes of Section 9 of the CPC. As has been explained earlier in this judgment, unlike a private arbitral forum agreed upon by and between contracting parties, in case of statutory arbitration, the arbitral tribunal vested with jurisdiction acquires the form of a statutory or administrative tribunal. It is a settled principle of jurisprudence under Section 9 of the CPC that the exclusion of the plenary jurisdiction of civil courts is not to be readily inferred and that any provision ousting such jurisdiction is to be strictly construed. It was held by the Supreme Court in Abbasia Cooperative Bank v. Hakeem Hafiz Muhammad Ghaus and Others (PLD 1997 Supreme Court 3) as follows: “The Civil Courts under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure are competent to try all suits of civil nature except those in which their jurisdiction is barred either expressly or by necessary implication. It is a well-settled principle of interpretation that the provision contained in a statute ousting the jurisdiction of Courts of general jurisdiction is to be construed very strictly and unless the case falls within the letter and spirit of the barring provision, it should not be given effect to.”

19. The principle that the ouster of the jurisdiction of civil courts is not to be readily inferred, and that ouster provisions are to be given a strict construction, applies with particular force to statutory arbitration. This is because the question before the Court is not one of giving effect to the autonomy and intent of the parties, but of construing statutory provisions in a manner that would create a statutory arbitral tribunal and thereby oust the jurisdiction of civil courts under Section 9 of the CPC. In order to do so, the following test must be satisfied:
i. The legislative intent must (a) explicitly vest jurisdiction in a specialized arbitral tribunal, and (b) make such dispute resolution process mandatory;
ii. In the absence of an arbitration agreement, the statute must define which disputes shall fall within the jurisdiction of the specialized arbitral tribunal for resolution;

iii. The statute should delineate the process and duty of appointing the arbitrator or tribunal vested with jurisdiction over the dispute, as the machinery provisions within the Arbitration Act for appointment of arbitrators rely on the intent and agreement of parties as evident from the arbitration agreement; and iv. where the jurisdiction vesting language in the statute is not explicit, or arbitration is mentioned as a mere possibility, as opposed to being mandated by determinative language, the plenary jurisdiction of civil courts under section 9 of CPC will not be deemed to have been ousted by implication.

20. In the facts of the case before us, Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules cannot be treated as forming part of the definition of “enactment” for the purposes of Section 46 of the Arbitration Act. Further, in order for Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules not to transcend the four corners of the PPRA Ordinance, and in view of the language of Rule 49, which is in the nature of a direction to the procuring agency to discharge an administrative duty, Rule 49 can only be treated as directory and not mandatory. Consequently, by virtue of Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules, disputes arising between a procuring agency and a contractor under a contract executed between them, which does not include an arbitration agreement, cannot be deemed to be the subject matter of mandatory arbitration. Accordingly, Rule 49 of the PPRA Rules neither provides for mandatory arbitration, which can only be provided through an explicit provision within an enactment, in this case the PPRA Ordinance, nor can the plenary jurisdiction of civil courts under Section 9 of the CPC be deemed to have been ousted on the basis of such a substatutory legal instrument.

21. For the aforementioned reasons, the instant appeal being devoid of merit is dismissed. However, the appellant shall be at liberty to seek an appropriate remedy before the Civil Courts in exercise of their plenary jurisdiction, if so advised.
